Why Teams Compare
Why teams compare Pepper alternatives

Pepper, from Pomegranate Technologies, sells an AI-first platform to independent distributors: a storefront, an Order Agent for order entry, and hubs for sales, finance, pricing and marketing. It is a lot of product. Here is where distributors start looking for something smaller.
The rollout runs into next quarter

Pepper publishes 35 to 90 days for a typical go-live, across five phases, with an implementation manager and a deployed engineer assigned. That is a fair number for the amount of platform it stands up. It is a long wait if what you wanted was orders arriving without a call to take.
You buy the whole stack to fix one step

Storefront, sales, finance, pricing, marketing. If your ERP suits you and your office runs fine, most of that is ground you already cover, and each module is another thing to configure, train and keep current.
The checking lands on your side

Order Agent reads the voicemail, text, photo or PDF the kitchen already sent. Pepper's own product page describes no step where the customer confirms what was read, so your order desk is the first person to see it written down.

They talk. It comes out as a list.

A chef counts the walk-in and says what is short. Each item turns into a line you can read, with the quantity beside it. Nothing to type, no time on hold, and no message for your team to interpret in the morning.
Press to speak, then read the lines back before sending

How VOS takes orders
Order Guides
Each account gets a list of its own

You hand over the guides each kitchen already buys from. VOS loads each one against your SKUs at the prices you hold for that account, so a spoken item lands on the right line and nobody guesses which pack was meant.
Each account sees only what it actually orders from you
Your prices, your SKUs, under your control, not the customer's
Change a guide once and it holds from then on
You keep the catalog; the customer gets the convenience

Delivery Formats
The order shows up in a shape you already handle
VOS does not ask your office to work somewhere new. Finished orders go out as email with a PDF, Excel or Word file, or straight into your ERP over the API, over EDI, or into QuickBooks.
Email goes to a rep or straight to your purchasing team
Nothing to retype over EDI, QuickBooks or the API
Your pick, invoice and delivery steps stay exactly as they are
Nothing in your stack has to come out first

Not Either Or
When VOS and Pepper work together
VOS is additive. Nothing has to come out for it to go in, so plenty of distributors run both.
Keep the storefront, add the voice
Some accounts are never going to browse a catalog. They will talk instead, at the end of a shift, from the walk-in. The storefront stays for the ones who tap, and VOS covers the ones who talk.
Try it on the accounts still phoning
VOS goes in beside what you run in a day or two, so you can put it on the handful of accounts that never adopted and judge it on those before you decide anything bigger.
The ERP keeps being the one destination
Both feed the system you have, so adding VOS does not change where an order ends up. It arrives over EDI, the API or QuickBooks, into the same place your team already works.
Watch one order travel from a kitchen to your desk
Book 20 minutes. We follow one spoken order all the way through to what your office opens, and you can judge the fit against anything else on your shortlist.

FAQ
Questions distributors ask when they compare the two
Is VOS a true Pepper alternative, and is it better than Pepper?

Those have the same answer: it depends what you are fixing. If the goal is to get orders off the phone and into something structured, VOS does that job, your customers approve each line themselves, and getting started does not take a quarter. If the goal is one platform running your storefront, your reps, your collections and your pricing, Pepper is built wide for that and VOS is not. We would rather say so now than at the demo.
How quickly can we actually be taking orders?

Most distributors reach that point in a day or two. There is no IT project here, and nothing to pull out of your stack, which is the main reason a Pepper alternative gets shortlisted at all. Pepper's own published window is a good deal longer, which is fair for the amount of platform it stands up.
Do we have to drop Pepper to bring VOS in?

No. VOS is additive by design and runs beside what you already have, so nothing needs switching off to try it. Plenty of distributors come to us with an ERP they like and a storefront they are keeping, and VOS covers how the order arrives.
Will VOS replace our ERP or order management system?

No, it does not. VOS is the way in: it gets the order from your customer to you, confirmed and itemized. From there it reaches your existing software or your inbox, and how you pick, bill and ship does not change.
What does VOS cost?

We quote by distributor, so tell us how many accounts you have and we will price it. Pepper quotes too, and publishes no rate card either, so a demo on both sides is the only way to compare the two fairly.
Do our customers need new hardware or a tablet?
No. VOS works on the iOS or Android phone the kitchen already has. We send nothing out, there is nothing to bolt to a counter, and no device for you to support.
What happens to the customers who still call their order in?

They can keep phoning, and your team handles those exactly as it does now. Worth being clear though: a call or a voicemail does not get a VOS order number, a timestamp or a stock movement. Only what comes through the app does.
Where do the Pepper details on this page come from?

Pepper's own website. The module list, the storefront and Order Agent descriptions and the 35 to 90 day implementation window were all read off usepepper.com on 10 October 2026, including their own post on how long an implementation takes. We have not repeated their marketing numbers here. If any of it has changed since, this page is the thing that is out of date, not them.
